title: multiplication and division facts to 100 (emerging computational fluency)

lesson.title: Multiplication and Division Facts to 100: Groups, Skips, and Splits

steps.say: Hi friend, it's Ms. Yuanyuan! Imagine you're helping set up snacks at a Grade 5 party in Kelowna. You have six little trays, and each tray holds seven granola bars. Your teacher asks, how many granola bars altogether? You could count them one by one, but that takes forever. Multiplication was invented for exactly this: counting equal groups quickly. Six groups of seven is forty-two granola bars.

visual.caption: 6 trays, 7 granola bars on each tray = 42

steps.say: Here's the first big idea. Multiplication is just repeated addition, but faster. Six sevens means seven plus seven plus seven plus seven plus seven plus seven. Let's add them up together: seven, fourteen, twenty-one, twenty-eight, thirty-five, forty-two. That's skip counting by sevens, and it lands on the very same answer, forty-two. So skip counting and multiplying are best friends.

visual.caption: Six jumps of 7 along the number line: 7, 14, 21, 28, 35, 42

steps.say: Now let's look for patterns, because patterns make facts stick without memorizing. On a hundred chart, circle the multiples of seven: seven, fourteen, twenty-one, twenty-eight, thirty-five, forty-two, forty-nine, fifty-six, sixty-three, seventy. See how they march down the chart in a slanted line? Every time you jump to the next one, you move down one row and back three squares. Patterns like this help you find a fact even when you can't remember it.

visual.caption: Multiples of 7 make a slanted path down the hundred chart

steps.say: Here's a lovely mental math trick called doubling. If you already know your twos, you get your fours and eights for free. Let's do four times eight. Start with two times eight, which is sixteen. Now double it: sixteen plus sixteen is thirty-two. So four times eight is thirty-two. Want eight times eight? Double thirty-two to get sixty-four. You climbed from an easy fact to a harder one just by doubling.

visual.caption: 4 groups of 8 dots = 32, which is double 2 groups of 8

steps.say: Another trick is splitting a hard fact into two easy ones. This is called the distributive property, but let's just call it breaking apart. Try seven times eight. Break the seven into five and two. Five times eight is forty, and two times eight is sixteen. Now add them: forty plus sixteen is fifty-six. So seven times eight is fifty-six. Look at the area picture, one rectangle split into two friendly pieces.

visual.caption: A 7 by 8 rectangle split into 5 rows (40) plus 2 rows (16) = 56

steps.say: Now the flip side: division. Say you have fifty-six blueberries from a Fraser Valley farm and you want to share them fairly into eight small containers. How many go in each? Instead of guessing, ask yourself a multiplication question: what times eight makes fifty-six? You already know it, seven! So fifty-six divided by eight is seven. Every multiplication fact secretly gives you two division facts. That's called a fact family.

visual.caption: Sharing 56 into 8 equal parts gives 7 in each part

steps.say: Let's try one slightly harder one together, with real dollars. Erin buys nine reusable water bottles for a class trip, and each bottle costs six dollars. What's the total? Break the nine into five and four. Five times six is thirty, and four times six is twenty-four. Thirty plus twenty-four is fifty-four dollars. And to check it, flip it into division: fifty-four dollars divided by nine bottles is six dollars each. Perfect, it matches.

visual.caption: Area model for 9 x 6 = 54, checked by 54 ÷ 9 = 6

steps.say: So remember, you don't have to memorize every fact by heart. You can skip count, you can double, you can break a number apart, and you can always flip a division back into a multiplication you already know. The more you play with these, the faster they come. You're doing beautifully!

lesson.answer: Multiplication is counting equal groups fast, and division just asks the same question backwards — skip count, double, or break apart to find any fact to 100.

practice.question: At a Vancouver farmers market, Maya buys 8 baskets of strawberries and each basket costs 7 dollars. How much does she spend in total? Then, if she paid with 56 dollars exactly and wants to check her answer, how much was each basket?
practice.answer: 8 times 7 equals 56 dollars in total. Checking with division: 56 divided by 8 equals 7 dollars per basket. (Tip: break it apart — 5 times 7 is 35, plus 3 times 7 is 21, and 35 plus 21 is 56.)
